metadata.title: Holistic exploration of reading comprehension skills, technology and socioeconomic factors in Spanish teenagers

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses publicly accessible PISA 2018 microdata for Spain, focusing on student background variables and reading test performance. The authors state that numerical variables are already scaled using weighted likelihood estimation (WLE), which is consistent with PISA’s complex survey scaling approach, but they do not report whether they applied student/sampling weights in the ML training stage. The manuscript also does not mention replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) or any explicit weight variable name (such as TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because the analysis is based on standard scikit-learn-style ML with one-hot encoding and 10-fold cross-validation, it is unclear whether complex survey design corrections were incorporated beyond the WLE scaling already applied to numeric scales.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that PISA 2018 microdata for Spain contains about 36,000 cases and that 22,400 (67%) contain all information needed for the study, implying a complete-case restriction. However, it does not explicitly describe how missingness was handled for the specific variables used in the ML models (e.g., whether any additional imputation was performed, or whether all models used only complete cases for every predictor). This is a reporting gap because missing-data handling can affect both model training and the stability of SHAP-based importance estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 microdata for Spain (students aged 15 years and 3 months to 16 years and 2 months at the start of the assessment period). The analytic dataset was restricted to cases containing all information needed for the study: 22,400 students (67%) out of about 36,000 microdata records. The focal variables were selected from student, school, and background questionnaires and reading performance; annual household income (PA042Q01TA) was excluded. The analysis further uses the selected categorical predictors (e.g., region, school type, gender, ICT-use categories) and numeric WLE-based scales (COMPICT, AUTICT), with one-hot encoding applied to categorical variables.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (Spain, age 15; reading comprehension PVREAD)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model selection via 10-fold cross-validation using RMSE; CatBoost selected as best algorithm. Exact RMSE values are not reported in the provided text; baseline and pairwise Wilcoxon significance comparisons are described qualitatively.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (Spain) the study leveraged Playing online games, Daily internet usage (week), Perceived ICT competence, Perceived ICT autonomy, and Mother’s education level to predict Reading comprehension skills (PVREAD mean), finding that online gaming frequency is the strongest negative contributor while moderate weekday internet use and positive ICT perceptions are associated with higher reading scores. This indicates that Spanish education and family guidance should prioritize time-limited, learning-oriented technology use and strengthen students’ perceived digital competence and autonomy, while cautioning against heavy online gaming exposure (causal effects cannot be inferred from cross-sectional ML).

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata for Spain, predicting students’ reading comprehension performance using PVREAD (mean reading test per student) as the outcome. It tests multiple supervised ML regressors (baseline, linear models, decision trees, Random Forest, AdaBoost, gradient boosting variants including XGBoost/LightGBM/Histogram GBR, and CatBoost, plus MLP and k-NN) and selects CatBoost as the best-performing model using 10-fold cross-validation with RMSE; exact RMSE values are not reported in the excerpt. The authors then use SHAP/Shapley-value post-hoc explainability to rank predictors and describe estimated impacts: playing online games shows the largest negative association (increasing frequency lowers reading), while weekday internet use shows a bell-shaped positive effect (roughly 1–4 hours/day) and perceived ICT competence/autonomy are positively related. The analysis uses one-hot encoding for categorical variables and notes WLE scaling for numeric variables, but it does not clearly report missing-data handling beyond restricting to cases with complete information, nor whether survey weights were applied in ML training. Therefore, results are best interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
